stem: A client with chronic kidney disease reports taking over-the-counter ibuprofen every day for musculoskeletal pain. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Regular NSAID use warrants clinician review because NSAIDs can reduce renal blood flow and worsen renal injury, especially when kidney function is impaired.
options.B: Daily ibuprofen is preferred in CKD because NSAIDs increase renal blood flow and protect remaining kidney function during long-term use.
options.C: Over-the-counter ibuprofen has minimal renal risk in CKD because nonprescription status indicates that daily long-term use is kidney-safe.
options.D: Higher ibuprofen doses are safer in CKD because stronger anti-inflammatory effects reduce the likelihood of NSAID-related renal injury.

rationale: Ibuprofen labeling states that long-term NSAID administration can cause renal injury and that prostaglandin inhibition can reduce renal blood flow, with greatest risk among patients with impaired renal function. Regular daily use in CKD therefore warrants clinician review. B and D reverse the renal-risk relationship, and C incorrectly equates OTC availability with kidney safety.
educational_objective: Recognize NSAID-related renal risk and the need to review regular ibuprofen use in a client with CKD.
source_version_date: Current DailyMed FDA label as accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: Warnings — Renal Effects and Advanced Renal Disease: long-term NSAID use can cause renal injury; reduced prostaglandin formation can reduce renal blood flow; risk is greatest in impaired renal function.
source_claim_supported: Daily NSAID use can worsen renal risk in CKD and merits clinician review rather than assumption of safety.

source_original.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease reports taking over-the-counter ibuprofen every day for musculoskeletal pain. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Regular NSAID use warrants clinician review because NSAIDs can reduce renal blood flow and worsen renal injury, especially when kidney function is impaired.
options.B: Daily ibuprofen is preferred in CKD because NSAIDs increase renal blood flow and protect remaining kidney function during long-term use.
options.C: Over-the-counter ibuprofen has minimal renal risk in CKD because nonprescription status indicates that daily long-term use is kidney-safe.
options.D: Higher ibuprofen doses are safer in CKD because stronger anti-inflammatory effects reduce the likelihood of NSAID-related renal injury.

source_original.rationale: FDA ibuprofen labeling warns that long-term NSAID use can cause renal injury and that prostaglandin inhibition can reduce renal blood flow, with greater risk in patients who already have impaired renal function. Option A therefore appropriately prompts review rather than assuming daily OTC use is safe. Options B and D reverse the renal-risk relationship. Option C incorrectly equates nonprescription availability with renal safety.
source_original.source_detail: DailyMed Ibuprofen Tablets — Warnings, Renal Effects/Advanced Renal Disease: long-term NSAID administration can cause renal injury; renal prostaglandin inhibition can reduce renal blood flow, with greatest risk in patients with impaired renal function; advanced renal disease requires avoidance or close renal monitoring when treatment is necessary. Current FDA ibuprofen tablet labeling at cited DailyMed set ID; Renal Effects/Advanced Renal Disease sections live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication routes, administration, reversal, adverse effects/interactions, withdrawal, monitoring and client teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained construct/key and preserved a clinician-review recommendation rather than overclaiming universal NSAID prohibition for all CKD.

audit_findings.claim_audit: No universal contraindication is asserted for all CKD.

distractor_audit.C: OTC status does not establish kidney safety
distractor_audit.D: Higher doses do not reduce renal risk
